slides.title: Motion Editing
slides.speech: So Go-with-the-Flow makes new videos. What about the video you already have? On top, a bichon and a corgi racing down a sidewalk, finishing about side by side. The dots and lines are point tracks, pink for the bichon's face, red for the corgi's. I want the corgi to win, so I drag its red track forward. The bottom row is the output. In the red box, the corgi's in front. Same dogs, same street, new motion. That's MotionV2V: editing the motion of a video that already exists.

slides.title: Why not GWTF?

elements.text: Anything not in frame 1 gets made up

slides.speech: So why can't GWTF do this? General point and flow motion control, ATI, ReVideo, and my own GWTF, is image-to-video. It takes this first frame and generates the rest. Anything that's not in frame one, like a car that drives in later, gets made up. And the classic editing trick, invert the video back to noise and regenerate it, needs the output to line up with the input frame by frame. Change the motion, and that breaks.

slides.title: Motion Counterfactuals
slides.speech: So we train a model, and the problem is data. You'd want pairs of videos with the same content and different motion, and those don't exist, so we make them. Start with a real video, this guy walking, and cut a clip out of it. That real clip is the target, what the model has to output. The target is always real, so the model learns to output real-looking video.

slides.title: Motion Counterfactuals

elements.text: Generated in-between, or real frames resampled

slides.speech: Then we make a fake version with different motion. That's a motion counterfactual. Two ways. Top right, a video model fills in between two real frames, with a prompt like make him twirl. Or we resample the real frames, faster, slower, reversed, so those pairs are real frames on both sides. Then crop and zoom on all of them, bottom right. To match points, we run one tracker and start points only on real frames both videos contain. For a generated clip, that's its two real end frames. So each dot should be the same physical point, as far as the tracker gets it right. Fake video and tracks in, real video out.

slides.title: The Model

elements.text: Frozen CogVideoX-5B + trained copy of its first 18 blocks, zero-init

slides.speech: At test time: a guy roasting a marshmallow next to a sleeping dog. I click points, a tracker follows them, and those are the source tracks. I drag them where I want them, and those are the target tracks, in the red box. The model gets each track as a colored blob on black, one color per point. It's a frozen CogVideoX, plus a trained copy of its first eighteen blocks, added back through zero-initialized layers. The target tracks line up with the output, like a normal ControlNet input. Your video doesn't. We think it works because these blocks attend across all frames. We didn't ablate that.

slides.title: Results

elements.text: Limits: about 20 points · copies on pixel-perfect points · chained edits drift · fake training inputs · 49 frames

slides.speech: On this basketball, the ball went through the hoop, but a second ball showed up where the original went. Plus or minus two pixels of noise at test time, not in training, fixed it. It's a shortcut: exact points means copy. User study: 41 people, 20 edits we made, pick the best of four. Ours got 69%, ATI 25, even on a stronger base model. For reconstruction, we cut each video at the middle. One half, reversed, is the input, the other half is the target, and both start on the middle frame, so image-to-video methods get a fair first frame. Reversal's in our training data, so this tests keeping content, not editing in general. SSIM is about 0.1 for everyone, since generated motion is never pixel-aligned, so L2 and LPIPS carry it. No error bars. Limits are on the bottom. We trained on 1 to 64 points, with more dropout on targets, and past about twenty it stops following. This is CVPR 2026, code's not out. Motion's one kind of edit. Next, I want any edit.
